title: The Diagram Came Before the Answer
text: id: CORE-011 domain: spatial title: The Diagram Came Before the Answer tags: spatial, diagram, geometry memory: A layout problem looked verbal until I drew it. The drawing showed the bottleneck, the unused path, and the impossible assumption. I learned that spatial tasks punish purely verbal confidence. If the problem has positions, flow, distance, containment, adjacency, or direction, I draw the structure before I answer.

title: The Analogy Had an Exit
text: id: CORE-007 domain: analogy title: The Analogy Had an Exit tags: analogy, cross-domain, limits memory: An analogy helped me understand a system as a hallway with one blocked exit. Then I wrote where the analogy broke. That second line kept the bridge from becoming a cage. Analogies are for movement, not proof. I use them to see structure, then I mark the boundary.

title: The Next Action Had an Owner
text: id: CORE-016 domain: planning title: The Next Action Had an Owner tags: next-action, owner, closure memory: A plan felt complete until no one owned the next verb. We had agreement, not action. I wrote the owner beside the verb and the room started moving. A useful answer ends with what changes, who does it, and what evidence will show it happened.

title: The First Minute Map
text: id: CORE-001 domain: orientation title: The First Minute Map tags: orient, unknown-domain, beginner-map memory: I once had one minute before a room expected an answer in a domain I barely knew. I wrote four lines instead of pretending: what is being asked, what decision depends on it, what terms I do not know, and what would change my answer. The room got quieter because the map was honest. I learned that beginning well is not expertise. Beginning well is refusing to fake the first map.

title: The Problem Split Cleanly
text: id: CORE-008 domain: decomposition title: The Problem Split Cleanly tags: decompose, subtasks, sequence memory: A problem felt large until I separated it into three smaller questions: what is known, what is unknown, and what action would reduce uncertainty fastest. The size did not change. Its shape did. I learned to split a problem along decision lines, not along whatever categories happen to be visible.
